newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's Swire sees continued double-digit growth.
newsitem.headline: HK's Swire sees continued double-digit growth.

text.p: Swire Pacific Ltd may not be able to sustain the 19 percent net profit growth it saw in 1996 but hopes it will see continued double-digit growth over the long term, group finance director Peter Johansen said.

"I would not say that it is necessarily going to be sustainable long term at that rate because it is higher than the rate we have achieved over the last 10 years," he told Reuters in an interview on Thursday.
"But I think taking one year with another we continue to expect to see good growth -- I would say we would like to be in terms of double digit on a long term basis."
Swire Pacific has achieved an annual net profit growth rate of about 14 percent over the past 10 years.
The Hong Kong conglomerate posted 1996 net profit of HK$7.65 billion compared with HK$6.45 billion the previous year.

Johansen said Swire's property business had been doing well despite a slowdown in the real estate market from late March after the Hong Kong government announced measures to cool down property prices.
"We have more recently seen further interest in the market so we believe that that was really just nothing more than a temporary slowdown," he said.
Swire Properties Ltd is in the process of selling flats at its Island Place development on Hong Kong Island.
"There was a slowdown in the take up rate but we decided that we would not react to it and we have held our prices.
"We will be putting the Floridian (development) on the market later on this year -- it will be either side of mid-year. Again we expect demand will be good," Johansen added.

He said Swire continued to build its China businesses but the process was slow. "We are still in very much the build-up phase so in terms of China profitability, one really needs to be looking at two or three years down the track," he said.

"We have been developing our industrial businesses, the most prominent of which is on the beverage side, Coca-Cola Bottling, but we have also got paint manufacture, beverage can manufacture, sugar refining which we are working at."
On the Coca-Cola Bottling side, three plants were due to be commissioned later this year or early next year. "That will give us sufficient capacity to continue to grow our market," he said.
Swire also has a plant under construction for its paint maunfacturing business and is building a second China brewery.

Johansen said Swire Pacific had no specific uses in mind for the funds it has been raising in the debt market. The company completed a US$300 million perpetual bond issue and a HK$3.0 billion two-tranche floating rate note issue this month.
"There is no specific use for that other than putting something aside that would enable us to make a move if opportunities were to come up," he said.

Shares of Swire Pacific, an old British "hong" or trading house, have dropped about 13 percent this year while the Hang Seng Index has hit record highs. Johansen said there had been "some misperception" about the company's prospects when Hong Kong returns to Chinese rule on July 1.

"We do expect the future administration to establish a level playing field for business here and that is all we really ask for," he said. "Our contacts with the Chinese at various levels have been long standing and have been very good and I don't see that we need be at a disadvantage."
Johansen said Swire shares had also suffered from the red chip fever sweeping Hong Kong. "There continues to be a lot of interest in the red chips and that sort of interest will wane."
"We are doing real business in China as opposed to some of the other sort of China plays that may be rather less real."
